context_blurb:
You know that a green plant builds its food from carbon dioxide and water, powered by light. Now follow the atoms. No atom is made or lost in a chemical reaction, so the atoms going in always match the atoms coming out. Tracing which atom goes where took 170 years, from a candle in a jar to algae fed heavy oxygen.

In symbols, photosynthesis is 6CO2 + 6H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6O2: six carbon dioxide molecules and six water molecules become one molecule of glucose, a sugar, and six oxygen molecules. Each formula counts one molecule's atoms, so CO2 holds one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms, H2O two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen, and C6H12O6 holds six carbon, twelve hydrogen and six oxygen. Carbon dioxide is the only thing going in that carries carbon, so each glucose takes six carbon dioxide molecules, and two glucose molecules take twelve, two times six.

Light has no formula in the equation, because it brings energy but no atoms: every atom of the glucose comes from the carbon dioxide and the water. A leaf cell does this work in its chloroplasts, tiny green bodies filled with chlorophyll, a pigment, or colouring substance, which catches the light and passes its energy straight on. That energy ends up stored in the glucose as chemical energy, energy held in the way its atoms are joined, and the plant can draw on it long after the light is gone.

An early clue came from a candle. Joseph Priestley burned one in a sealed jar until its flame died, and on 17 August 1771 he set a sprig of mint inside that spoiled air and kept the jar shut. On the 27th, ten days on, a new candle, lit in the same air, burned perfectly well: the mint had mended the air the first flame had spoiled. He also split spoiled air in two and gave a plant to one part only, and a candle burned only in that part. Plants, he concluded, restore air that burning spoils; the mint, we now know, was giving off the oxygen a flame needs.

In the early 1880s the German biologist Theodor Engelmann found where the oxygen is made, and by which light. Under his microscope he laid a thread of green alga, whose cells hold chloroplasts as a leaf's do, among bacteria that gather wherever oxygen is richest, then used a prism to fan sunlight into a rainbow along it. The bacteria crowded thickest around the alga's chloroplasts, most of all where red and blue light fell, for there the oxygen poured out fastest. Chlorophyll soaks up red and blue light most strongly and takes in little green, which is why leaves look green and why the bacteria were fewest in the green and yellow.

Chemists had long believed that a plant's oxygen came from its carbon dioxide, which holds more oxygen than water does. Cornelis van Niel doubted it in 1931. The purple bacteria he studied use light to build their food from carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulfide (H2S), which is built like water (H2O) but with sulfur in place of oxygen, and they give off sulfur where plants give off oxygen. That sulfur can only come from the hydrogen sulfide, so, he reasoned, a plant's oxygen must come from its water.

In 1941 at the University of California, Martin Kamen, Samuel Ruben and two co-workers tested his idea with oxygen-18, or heavy oxygen. It is an isotope, a form of an element whose atoms hold a different number of neutrons: ten instead of the usual eight, so its atoms weigh a little more and can be told apart. One batch of algae got water rich in heavy oxygen; a second got carbon dioxide loaded with it. Only the algae with the heavy-oxygen water gave off oxygen rich in heavy atoms, in the same share as their water held, so a plant's oxygen comes from the water it splits. The textbook equation is only a net count, what is left once the ins and outs cancel: to free six oxygen molecules, which hold twelve oxygen atoms, a plant splits twelve water molecules and makes six new ones.
